summary.text: Take \(n=8=2^3\), for which \(\Omega(8)=3\) is odd and at least \(3\). Möbius inversion gives \(a(8)=8!\bigl(H_8-H_4\bigr)=25584>0\), contradicting the predicted negative sign.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j
\]
be the \(n\)-th harmonic number. The sequence \(a(n)\) is characterized by
\[
\sum_{k\mid n}\frac{a(k)}{k!}=H_n.
\]
Put \(b(k)=a(k)/k!\). Then the defining relation is
\[
\sum_{k\mid n}b(k)=H_n.
\]
By Möbius inversion,
\[
b(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)H_d,
\]
where \(\mu\) is the ordinary Möbius function. Consequently,
\[
a(n)=n!\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)H_d.
\]

We disprove the proposed universal equivalence by taking \(n=8\). This is a positive integer, and its positive divisors are
\[
1,2,4,8.
\]
Therefore the Möbius-transform formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(8)
&=8!\bigl(\mu(8)H_1+\mu(4)H_2+\mu(2)H_4+\mu(1)H_8\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Recall that \(\mu(m)=0\) when \(m\) is divisible by the square of a prime, \(\mu(p)=-1\) for a prime \(p\), and \(\mu(1)=1\). Since both \(8\) and \(4\) are divisible by \(2^2\), while \(2\) is prime, we have
\[
\mu(8)=0,\qquad \mu(4)=0,\qquad \mu(2)=-1,\qquad \mu(1)=1.
\]
Thus
\[
a(8)=8!\,(H_8-H_4).
\]
The difference of these harmonic numbers is
\[
H_8-H_4=\frac15+\frac16+\frac17+\frac18.
\]
Using the common denominator \(840\),
\[
\frac15+\frac16+\frac17+\frac18
=\frac{168+140+120+105}{840}
=\frac{533}{840}.
\]
Since \(8!=40320=48\cdot840\), it follows that
\[
a(8)=40320\cdot\frac{533}{840}=48\cdot533=25584.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(8)>0,
\]
so the assertion \(a(8)<0\) is false.

On the other hand, \(\Omega(n)\) denotes the total number of prime factors of \(n\), counted with multiplicity. Because
\[
8=2^3,
\]
we have
\[
\Omega(8)=3.
\]
The number \(3\) is odd and is at least \(3\). Hence, at \(n=8\), the right-hand side of the proposed equivalence—“\(\Omega(n)\) is odd and at least \(3\)”—is true, while the left-hand side—“\(a(n)<0\)”—is false.

Therefore
\[
a(n)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(\Omega(n)\text{ is odd and }\Omega(n)\ge3\bigr)
\]
does not hold for every positive integer \(n\). The conjecture is false.
